rejected.title: Remedies in civil cases
card: A remedy is what a court orders when the plaintiff wins a civil case. Most remedies aim to restore the plaintiff, as far as possible, to the position they were in before the wrong.
Damages
a sum of money paid to the plaintiff. Most damages compensate for loss, such as lost income, medical bills or damage to property. Exemplary damages are rarer and can punish very serious misconduct.
Injunction
a court order that tells a party to stop doing something, or to do something. It deals with the problem itself, not with money.
A court picks the remedy that suits the harm. Money cannot always fix a wrong, such as ongoing noise, so an injunction may be ordered instead of damages, or together with them.
rejected.remember: Damages are money, mostly to compensate for loss. An injunction orders a party to stop or to act.

a.q: Which of these is an injunction?
opts: An order that a factory stop running machines at night
An order that a driver pay $8000 for a damaged fence
An order that a landlord pay a tenant's lost income
An order that a company pay for a customer's medical bills
a.why: An injunction is an order to stop doing something or to do something, and a night-time ban on machines is a direct order to stop. The other three orders are payments of money for loss, which are damages.
a.clue: Look for the order about conduct, not a payment.

b.q: Priya's neighbour Tom keeps building a wall that blocks her light, and she has lost rent from a tenant who left. She sues and wins. Which remedies fit her case?
opts: An injunction to stop the wall, and damages for the rent
Damages only, because rent loss is the only harm
An injunction only, because the wall is still going up
Damages to stop the wall, and an injunction for the rent
b.why: The wall is an ongoing problem, so an injunction can order Tom to stop. The lost rent is a money loss, so damages can compensate for it. The last option swaps the two: damages are money, and an injunction deals with conduct, not with paying for a loss.
b.clue: One harm is still happening and one is a past money loss.

draft.title: Remedies in civil cases
card: A remedy is what a court orders to put right a wrong when the plaintiff wins a civil case. The aim is to fix the harm, not to punish the defendant.
Damages
a sum of money paid to the plaintiff to compensate for loss, such as lost income, medical bills or damage to property.
Injunction
a court order that tells a party to stop doing something, or to do something. It deals with the problem itself, not with money.
A court picks the remedy that suits the harm. Money cannot always fix a wrong, such as ongoing noise, so an injunction may be ordered instead of damages, or together with them.
draft.remember: Damages pay for loss. An injunction orders a party to stop or to act.

a.q: Which of these is an injunction?
opts: An order that a factory stop running machines at night
An order that a driver pay $8000 for a damaged fence
An order that a landlord refund a tenant's lost income
An order that a company pay for a customer's medical bills
a.why: An injunction is an order to stop doing something or to do something, and a night-time ban on machines is a direct order to stop. The other three orders are payments of money for loss, which are damages.
a.clue: Look for the order about conduct, not a payment.

b.q: Priya's neighbour Tom keeps building a wall that blocks her light, and she has lost rent from a tenant who left. She sues and wins. Which remedies fit her case?
opts: An injunction to stop the wall, and damages for the rent
Damages only, because rent loss is the only harm
An injunction only, because the wall is still going up
Damages to punish Tom, and an injunction to pay her costs
b.why: The wall is an ongoing problem, so an injunction can order Tom to stop. The lost rent is a money loss, so damages can compensate for it. Damages only would leave the wall in place, and damages do not aim to punish.
b.clue: One harm is still happening and one is a past money loss.

a.best: An order that a factory stop running machines at night

b.best: An injunction to stop the wall, and damages for the rent

problems.detail: The card says the aim of a remedy is 'to fix the harm, not to punish the defendant', and defines damages only as compensation. Exemplary (punitive) damages exist in Victoria and are meant to punish, and the VCE study design covers the types of damages. This overgeneralisation is false as stated.

The why says 'damages do not aim to punish'. That is false for exemplary (punitive) damages. The option 'Damages to punish Tom...' is still wrong, but only because an injunction does not order costs to be paid. The explanation should not deny that damages can ever punish.

a.q: A court orders a party to stop running loud machines at night. Which remedy is this, and why?
opts: An injunction, because it orders a party to stop conduct
Damages, because it compensates for the harm of the noise
An injunction, because it orders a payment to the plaintiff
Damages, because it punishes a party for serious misconduct
a.why: An order to stop conduct is an injunction, because it deals with the problem itself and not with money. Damages are a payment, so an order to stop running machines is not damages, even though it responds to harm.
a.clue: Think about what the order actually requires the party to do.

opts: An injunction to stop the noise, and damages for the rent
Damages only, because the lost rent is the only harm
An injunction only, because the noise is still going on
Damages to stop the noise, and an injunction for the rent
b.why: The noise is an ongoing problem, so an injunction can order Tom to stop. The lost rent is a money loss, so damages can compensate for it. The option with damages to stop the noise and an injunction for the rent swaps the two: damages are money, and an injunction deals with conduct, not with paying for a loss.
b.clue: One harm is still happening and one is a past money loss.
